source_text: Ἐν ᾧ ἄν τις δύναιτο εὖ ποιεῖν τοῖς πλησίον καὶ οὐ ποιεῖ· ἀλλότριος τῆς ἀγάπης τοῦ Κυρίου νομισθήσεται. Hoc attulit
thought_title: Failure to do good estranges from the Lord's love
orientation: Irenaeus closes the letter with a general warning about failing to do good to a neighbor.
pass_a_gloss: In whatever matter anyone might be able to do good to neighbors and does not do it, he will be considered a stranger to the love of the Lord. Hoc attulit

choices.why: The glossary bans 'charity of the Lord' and 'love of Christ'; 'stranger' preserves the sense of being alienated or outside the love of the Lord.
The passive future of νομίζω carries the sense of being reckoned or judged as; 'will be considered' keeps the impersonal judgment force.
The relative with ἐν indicates the sphere or matter in which the failure occurs; 'in whatever matter' preserves the generalizing force.
The infinitive phrase is the standard Greek idiom for benefaction; 'to do good' is literal and clear.

pass_b_english: If someone is able to do good to their neighbors and does not do it, that person will be considered a stranger to the love of the Lord. Irenaeus concluded with this saying.
notes: The Latin phrase 'Hoc attulit' appears after the Greek and is not part of the Greek sentence; it is likely a scribal or editorial note meaning 'He brought this' or 'This he adduced.'

problems.fix: If someone is able to do good to their neighbors and does not do it, that person will be considered a stranger to the love of the Lord. He brought this.
